svg.aria-label: Diagram: the defining properties of a Google Cloud emergency access user, four standard security practices that invert for break-glass accounts and the documented reason for each, the physical and split storage design for credentials and security keys, and the detection you must build yourself
svg.title: Break-glass accounts: where the standard security practices invert, and why
svg.text: The one place where four standard best practices are documented in reverse.
Because the risk being managed is losing access, and the usual tooling becomes a privileged attack path.
What an emergency access user is, by definition
Created in your Cloud Identity account, holding the super admin privilege.
NOT associated with a specific employee, so exempt from the Joiner/Mover/Leaver lifecycle.
Exempt from SSO, on purpose, so an IdP outage cannot lock you out.
A single one is a single point of failure. Recommended: minimum TWO, maximum FIVE per account.
Four standard practices that invert for these accounts
Normally
For break-glass
Because
Keep secrets in a password manager
Physical controls
it must work during an outage
Automate password rotation
Rotate by hand
the rotator would need super admin
Expire passwords
Disable expiration
unless you rotate manually
Enforce SSO and device policy
Exempt at least one
the control can lock you out
The storage design is physical, and deliberately split
Enroll TWO OR MORE FIDO security keys per user; allow ONLY security keys as the 2SV method.
Store copies of passwords in multiple security vaults in different offices.
Store the password and the security keys in DIFFERENT locations.
Detection, and two different things called breakglass
Any activity outside an emergency likely indicates suspicious behaviour. Alert on the OU,
threshold every 1 hour when count is above 0. You must build this; nothing fires by itself.
Contrast: Binary Authorization breakglass logs itself to Cloud Audit Logs either way.
Also: SSO users are NOT required to do Google 2SV by default. Turn on post-SSO verification.
#55 said the super admin cannot be constrained by IAM. This is what you do instead:
two to five accounts, hardware keys in separate safes, no automation, and an alert you wrote.
The uncomfortable part is that the strongest control in a cloud security design is a locked
cabinet in an office, and the second strongest is somebody noticing it was opened.
